verses.translation_literal: A psalm, of Asaph. O God, nations have come into your inheritance; they have made unclean the temple of your holiness; they have made Jerusalem into heaps.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of Asaph, sung over ruins. O God, the nations have walked into your own inheritance. They have fouled the temple of your holiness with their feet and their hands, and Jerusalem, city of your name, lies where they made it: nothing but heaps of stone.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open on the shock of the opening verb: 'they have come.' The psalm starts in mid-catastrophe, with no greeting and no praise, and the singer says 'O God' the way a person calls out a name at a graveside. The enemy is simply 'nations' (goyim), a word that is not an insult but a category: peoples outside Israel's covenant. The first charge is not murder or plunder but contamination, because the temple was the place where a holy God dwelt among a people. Foreign soldiers inside it was an offense against holiness itself.

The KJV 'the heathen' adds a religious sneer the Hebrew lacks, and it softens the verb: 'defiled' sounds like a stain on cloth, where 'made unclean' (timme'u) is ritual language, the same word used of corpse and disease contamination. 'Thy holy temple' also flattens a Hebrew construct: 'the temple of your holiness.' Finally 'laid Jerusalem on heaps' hides a wordplay on sound: the closing 'le-ʿiyyim' is the plural of ʿi, a ruin mound, and Radak and Metzudat David explain it as heaps of stones, which is what a razed city looks like in the ancient Near East: a tell, a low hill of rubble. Play the line as a person looking out over it.

philological_notes.note: Ritual impurity, not mere dirt. The temple, the place of maximal holiness, is made unclean by the presence of the uncircumcised and of corpses, so the sin is cultic as much as political.

Plural of 'i, a ruin-heap; the same word appears in Micah 1:6 for ploughed-up ruins. Rashi and Radak read it as gelim, piles of stones; Ibn Ezra offers also 'low places' and a dig for buried treasure.

verses.translation_literal: They have given the corpse of your servants as food to the birds of the heavens, the flesh of your faithful ones to the living things of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: They left the bodies of your servants where they fell, and the sky took them. The birds of heaven came down to feast, and the flesh of your faithful ones went to the wild beasts of the land.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is nathnu, 'they have given,' as if the enemy offered the dead as a meal, so the bodies become gifts to scavengers. In ancient Israel and the wider Near East, being left unburied was among the worst of curses, found in covenant curses (Deut 28:26) and treaty texts, because it denied the dead rest and honor. The two halves of the verse are a pair, and each uses a different word for the dead: 'nivlat' (a corpse, a carcass) and 'basar' (flesh). Malbim's remark that the flesh was cut up and thrown out follows this contrast.

The KJV 'saints' and 'thy servants' make the victims sound pious and distant; the Hebrew 'chasidim' means those bound to God by covenant loyalty (chesed), and the poet claims them as his own. 'Fowls of the heaven' and 'beasts of the earth' are archaic: it is the whole sky and the whole land, a merism, with no corner left unprofaned. Radak adds that 'lechayto' has an extra vav for the same word, a point of grammar only; the sense is unchanged. Rashi reads 'chasidim' as the sinners who became faithful by accepting punishment, a rabbinic reading; the plain sense of the psalm does not need it.

philological_notes.note: Those who practice or receive covenant loyalty (chesed); KJV 'saints' is an anachronism. Rashi reads them as sinners made faithful by punishment; Radak says there were truly pious people among the exiles, such as Daniel and his companions.
A corpse or carcass, the word used for the unclean dead body; it sharpens the horror of leaving it to birds.

verses.translation_literal: They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there is none burying.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their blood was poured out like water, poured in streets and fields and all around Jerusalem, and no one came to bury them. No one at all.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Shafkhu' is the verb for pouring a liquid from a vessel, and the simile 'like water' is meant to shock: blood is life (Gen 9:4-6, Lev 17:11), and here it is treated as cheap as water in a land where water is precious. The scene is not a battlefield far off but 'round about Jerusalem,' the sacred place itself. Ibn Ezra notes that to pour blood like water means the killers did so with no fear that anyone would require it of them.

The last two words, 've-ein qover,' are blunt: 'and there is none burying.' It is a participle: not 'there was no one who buried them' in the KJV's past tense with a gentle 'them' added, but a flat present picture of an empty scene. Metzudat David says the survivors were too afraid to leave hiding to bury; Malbim says the desolation was so great. For an audience for whom burial was a sacred duty and the family tomb a mark of belonging, this is the most terrible silence in the verse. Let it hang.

philological_notes.note: 'And there is none burying': a participle after 'ein', which gives an unbroken present state. The absence of a burier is the point, not only the lack of graves.

verses.translation_literal: We have become a reproach to our neighbors, mockery and derision to those around us.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so we have become what they call across the fence: a reproach to the people next door, a joke for the ones who live all around us. Their laughter carries over the rubble, and it does not stop.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the horror of the unburied dead in verse 3, the psalm turns from bodies to faces: the neighbors watching. In the ancient Near East honor was public and shared, and a people whose god had apparently failed to defend its land and temple became a laughingstock, because a defeated nation meant a defeated deity. So this is more than hurt feelings. It prepares the question of verse 10, "Where is their God?" The actors should play the shame as something heard, a murmur that grows from the next village to the whole horizon.

The Hebrew stacks three words of contempt, cherpah, la'ag and qeles, and the second pair is a near-synonym doublet. The KJV renders la'ag "scorn" and qeles "derision" and so keeps the pile-up, but it flattens the progression: reproach is the insult, mockery is the laugh, and qeles is derision that turns into a byword. Rashi reads qeles as speech, "talking about them" (compare "for a byword", Deut 28:37). The KJV's "them that are round about us" is fine for the sense, but the Hebrew has the plain noun "our surroundings", the same word as in the neighbors/surrounders pair, so "neighbors" and "those around us" are two circles of onlookers. Malbim draws the distinction: those living among us, and those living around us.

philological_notes.note: Derision, mocking praise: the root also gives the verb 'to jeer', so the word suggests ridicule that is almost a performance. The noun is paired with reproach in Jer 20:8 and with 'mockery' in Ps 44:14; Metzudat Zion compares the related form qallasah in Ezek 22:4. Rashi takes it as speech about the people, a byword.
The same root returns in verse 12 as the verb 'they reproached you': what the neighbors hurled at Israel is what Israel asks to be returned to them, and what they hurled at God.

verses.translation_literal: Until what, YHWH? Will you be angry to perpetuity? Will your jealousy burn like fire?
verses.translation_dramatic: How long, LORD? How long? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy go on burning like fire, with nothing left to burn?
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns from description to the cry every lament has: 'ad-mah, YHWH' ('until what?'), shortened from 'ad matay' ('how long?'). This is the first time the personal name of God is spoken in the psalm; until now it was only the general 'Elohim.' The speaker moves from a distant, general power to the covenant God who made promises. The KJV 'Lord' hides this: in the KJV tradition small capitals mark the name, but the effect on the ear is lost. Say the name, then stop.

Two images of anger: 'te'enaf' (from 'af', the nose, which flares in anger, as in 'his nose burned' elsewhere), and the jealousy ('qin'ah') that burns 'like fire.' KJV 'jealousy' is correct, and it is a good word: it is the zeal of a spouse whose bond has been violated, the quality attached to the 'El qanna' of Exodus 20:5, as Rashi says. Ibn Ezra adds a dark twist: God was jealous because Israel served other gods, so why not be jealous of the foreigners? Radak notes that though the exile of 70 years was short, to the sufferers it seemed endless.

philological_notes.note: From the root for 'nose, anger'; a verb only used of God's anger (or of that of rulers), and it paints the flaring nostril. Rashi glosses it 'be wrathful'.
Jealousy or zeal for exclusive loyalty, the quality of the 'El qanna' of Exodus 20:5; Rashi ties it to that title.

verses.translation_literal: Pour out your wrath to the nations that do not know you, and upon kingdoms that on your name have not called.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pour it out. The anger that has burned like fire on us, pour it out on the nations that never knew you, on the kingdoms that never once called upon your name.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the lament, where the weeping turns into a demand. The speakers are the survivors of a wrecked city, and the verb is an imperative: shefokh, "pour out", the verb of verse 3's blood. The blood of the people was poured out like water; now they ask that the wrath be poured out in turn. The actors should not play this as a cry of rage, but as an argument. Its logic is the logic of covenant: the nations have not known you, we have; if there must be anger, let it fall where there is no relationship to betray. Radak says so outright: "we, even though we have sinned, knew you and called you by your name."

The KJV's "the heathen" belongs to its century. The Hebrew goyim is simply "nations", and the verse defines them not by religion in the abstract but by one thing, that they do not know you, a verb of relationship, not of information. The two halves are a standard parallel pair: nations, then kingdoms; not knowing, then not calling on the name. The preposition shifts from el to al, "to" then "upon"; the commentators treat them as equals (Radak, Metzudat Zion: el means al), and Meiri cites the parallel el heharim lo akhal, "he has not eaten upon the mountains" (Ezek 18:6), and Ibn Ezra a second, el yesod hamizbeach. The Targum sharpens the targets: star-worshippers, and the kingdoms of the Chaldeans. Almost the same wording stands in Jer 10:25, in the mouth of another city under siege.

philological_notes.note: The preposition el here has the force of al, 'upon'. Radak and Metzudat Zion say so directly; Meiri adds the parallel 'el heharim lo akhal' (Ezek 18:6), and Ibn Ezra, on the second half of the line, 'el yesod hamizbeach'.
'To know' in the covenant sense is to be in a relationship, to acknowledge. The parallel clause, 'have not called on your name', makes the same point as a deed: knowing is shown by calling.

verses.translation_literal: For it has eaten Jacob, and his habitation they have laid desolate.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he has devoured Jacob. They have eaten him alive, and left his dwelling desolate and empty.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Ki' (for) gives the reason for the prayer: the nations did not stop at conquest. The verb is 'akhal,' to eat, and it is singular, while the second verb 'heshammu' is plural. KJV, ASV and Webster smooth the singular into 'they have devoured,' hiding the shift; YLT keeps 'one hath devoured.' Meiri reads the singular as the wicked king at the head of the enemy and the plural as the whole host. The image is a predator swallowing a victim whole; it comes from the same family as verse 2's feast of birds and beasts, and the people themselves become the meal.

'Jacob' is the name the poem uses for the people as a whole, the chosen line, and 'navehu' is the pasture-dwelling or the shepherd's abode, a word with overtones of the temple as the home of God (Metzudat David reads it as the temple). Malbim adds that God's own anger spent itself on the wood and stones, so for the enemy to eat the people too was to go beyond what had been decreed. Ibn Ezra says: not enough that they did not know you; they ate those who do.

philological_notes.note: Singular 'he/it has eaten', while the verb 'they have laid waste' that follows is plural; the number shift is real and is kept in the literal layer. Meiri takes the singular for the enemy's king.
A shepherd's pasture or dwelling place; Metzudat David takes it as the temple.

verses.translation_literal: Do not remember to us the iniquities of the former [ones]; quickly may your compassions come to meet us, for we have become very low.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not hold the guilt of those who came before against us. Let your mercies run to meet us, and run quickly, for we are brought down, brought very low.
verses.directors_commentary:
The prayer turns inward from the enemy to the people's own record, and the ambiguity of 'avonot rishonim' is the verse's hinge. It can mean 'the sins of the former ones' (the ancestors, the reading of ASV and BBE and Ibn Ezra, as in the old claim that a generation pays for its fathers) or 'former sins' (the KJV reading, Radak and Meiri: sins of earlier years, 'sins of youth'). The Hebrew keeps both open, and the actor should not choose too early.

The verb 'yeqaddemunu' is lovely: the root is 'to be in front,' to go before someone and meet them. KJV 'prevent' is an archaic sense meaning 'go before,' which a modern reader will misread as 'stop.' The mercies (rachamim) are pictured as running out to meet a returning child, a word from the root for 'womb.' Metzudat David and Radak read 'dalonu' as poverty and lack of strength to bear the exile; the root dalal means to hang low, to be thin, like a dried-up stream. Malbim wrestles with the logic: if you remember the sins you will not show mercy, so let mercy arrive first.

philological_notes.note: Either iniquities of the forefathers or earlier iniquities of the speakers' own past; Ibn Ezra prefers the former, Radak and Meiri the latter ('sins of youth').
'May they go before us / meet us'; the KJV's 'prevent' reflects the older English sense of 'come before', not 'stop'. Radak glosses it as preparing a thing and bringing it before a person.
'We have become low or thin'; poverty and weakness together. Radak and Metzudat David read it as having no strength left to bear the exile.

token_glosses.gloss: may they come to meet us

verses.translation_literal: Help us, God of our salvation, on the matter of the glory of your name; and deliver us, and atone on our sins, for the sake of your name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Help us, God of our salvation, for the sake of the glory of your name. Rescue us, and cover our sins over, for your name's sake, for your name alone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The petition changes ground: the people stop pleading their need and plead God's reputation. 'Name' appears twice, once in 'the glory of your name' and again at the close ('for the sake of your name'), so the verse is framed by it. In the ancient Near East a god's name was bound to his standing among the nations, and a god who could not protect his people was a god mocked. The speaker uses this as an argument: act for yourself, if not for us. Radak and Meiri say plainly: your name is profaned among the nations.

Three verbs, three steps: help ('azrenu'), rescue ('hatzilenu'), and 'kapper,' which KJV renders 'purge away' and ASV 'forgive.' Neither is exact. Kapper is the ritual word of atonement, to cover or wipe over (the root of Yom Kippur), and the preposition is 'al,' 'on' or 'over' the sins, as one covers a stain. YLT's 'cover over' is closest. 'Al devar' is idiomatic, 'on the matter of,' hence 'for the sake of' (Metzudat Zion compares Numbers 25:18).

philological_notes.note: Imperative of the piel of kpr, the cultic word for atonement ('cover over'), with 'al' of the thing covered. KJV 'purge away' and ASV 'forgive' paraphrase; YLT 'cover over' is closest.
'On the matter of' or 'for the sake of'; Metzudat Zion cites Numbers 25:18 for the same idiom.

verses.translation_literal: Why should the nations say, Where is their God? Let it be made known among the nations before our eyes, the vengeance of the blood of your servants that was poured out.
verses.translation_dramatic: Why should the nations say, Where is their God? Let it be known among them, and let us see it with our own eyes: the vengeance for the blood of your servants, the blood that was poured out.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Where is their God?' is the taunt of the victor over the defeated, and it is the heart of the matter. In the ancient world, when a city fell its god was assumed to have fallen with it, and the conquerors would carry off or mock the idols. The poem repeats the question as the nations would speak it: 'ayyeh elohehem,' with 'Elohim' now used for the God of Israel in a foreigner's mouth. The KJV's 'their God' keeps this, but the stress should fall on the taunt, not the question.

The second half begins with a request in the passive: 'yivvada',' 'let it be known.' KJV and ASV rearrange this and the vengeance clause so the English reads smoothly; the Hebrew holds the clause back to the end, 'the vengeance of the blood of your servants that was poured out,' and the last word 'hashafukh' echoes verse 3's pouring. Ibn Ezra reads 'before our eyes' as 'while we are still alive'; the vengeance must come soon. Malbim: the two reasons together, a profaned name and the unavenged blood, are both concerns for God's honor.

philological_notes.note: Vengeance, in the legal sense of redress for blood that has been shed, not blind revenge; the blood of the servants was to be avenged on those who shed it.
'To our eyes': Ibn Ezra reads this as before we die, so the vengeance must come in the speakers' lifetime.

verses.translation_literal: May the groaning of the prisoner come before you; according to the greatness of your arm, leave over the sons of death.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the groan of the prisoner reach you. By the sheer greatness of your arm, keep alive those who are marked for death.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the dead and the mocked, the poem now looks at the captives, men in chains, awaiting execution or exile. 'Anaqah' is not speech but a sound: groaning, sighing, the noise a man makes in a cell. The psalm asks that sound to 'come before your face,' as a petition would be carried into a king's presence. It is a prayer without words. Metzudat Zion links it to the groan of the slain in Ezekiel 26:15.

'According to the greatness of your arm' points at the arm of YHWH that brought Israel out of Egypt: the same strength is asked again. The last phrase, 'bnei temutah,' literally 'sons of dying' or 'sons of death,' is rendered by the KJV 'those that are appointed to die.' That is a paraphrase, and a fair one; YLT's 'sons of death' is closer. Rashi compares the rabbinic phrase 'basar temutah' for an animal at death's door, so the 'sons' are those already on the brink. The verb 'hoter' ('leave over') can also be read as 'loose' (Ibn Ezra's alternative, Rashi's reading, from the verb for releasing bonds), a pun the Hebrew allows: leave them alive, or set them free.

philological_notes.note: 'Sons of dying': those who are condemned, or on the brink of death. Rashi compares the rabbinic 'basar temutah' for an animal on the point of dying (b. Qiddushin 21b-22a).

Hiphil of yatar, 'leave over, spare'. Rashi, the Metzudot and a view cited in Ibn Ezra read it as 'loosen' (from nattar), which fits the image of bound prisoners; the two readings give different pictures, preserved or freed.

verses.translation_literal: And return to our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, which they reproached you, O Lord.
verses.translation_dramatic: And pay it back to our neighbors, seven times over, into their own laps: the insults they threw, the ones they threw at you. O Lord, let it be returned.
verses.directors_commentary:
The neighbors of verse 4 return, and so does their word. Israel had been their reproach; now the reproach is theirs to receive, and the psalm changes whose insult it is: not what they said about us, but what they said about you. The prayer moves from "our" shame to God's, the same step as "for the glory of your name" in verse 9. The actors should hear the pivot at the last two words, "which they reproached you", where the grievance leaves the speakers and lands on God.

Shiv'atayim is a dual form, literally "two sevens" or "seven times over", and in biblical idiom seven is the number of completeness, as Metzudat David says ("many times"); Malbim argues that no equal measure exists between the Almighty and mortals, hence the surplus. The KJV's "render" is a fair word for hashev ("turn back, return"), and "sevenfold" is exact. The picture "into their bosom" is the fold of the garment at the chest, where something received is laid (compare Isa 65:6); Metzudat David reads it as retribution that goes straight to its target and does not swerve. BBE's "breast" is closer to the body than the KJV, but the KJV keeps the image. The line closes with Adonai, "my Lord", a title new in this psalm after Elohim (verse 1) and YHWH (verse 5), and here it carries the tone of a servant addressing a master whose honor has been insulted.

philological_notes.note: A dual form of 'seven': 'seven times over', not simply a multiple. Metzudat David glosses it 'two times seven, that is, many times'; Malbim explains the surplus: no measure is equal between God and those who insult him.
The bosom: the fold of the garment at the chest, where something received is laid. Metzudat David says the repayment goes straight into their lap and does not turn aside.

verses.translation_literal: And we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you for ever; to a generation and a generation we will recount your praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: But we are yours. Your people, the flock you pasture, and we will thank you for ever. From one generation to the next, we will tell it, we will tell your praise.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a quiet "and we", set against the "they" who have filled it. After the curses and the cry for blood, the speakers do not threaten; they promise. The image is the shepherd's: "sheep of your pasture" puts the survivors back in the care of the one they have been accusing, and the verbs are in the future, a vow the speakers make before the rescue. Play it low and steady, as a people choosing to be loyal in a ruin.

The KJV opens with "So", which the Hebrew does not have: it reads as the result of the prayers, a bargain ("if you save us, we will thank you"). The Hebrew has a plain "and we", which sets Israel against the nations rather than offering them as payment, though Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra do read thanks as following deliverance. "Shew forth" for nesapper is archaic and weak: the verb is "to recount, to tell", a spoken narration handed down. Malbim ties it to the shame of verse 4: the praise recounted is the answer to the reproach the neighbors told. The pair le'olam and ledor vador, "for ever" and "generation and generation", says the thanks will outlast the exile that the psalm opens with.

philological_notes.note: 'We will recount, tell': the piel of the root that also means 'count' and 'book'. The praise is a narration passed down by speech. Malbim glosses the praise as 'telling your praise'; the Targum renders the verb with a verb of declaring (netanei), not of showing.

'The sheep of your pasture': a covenant image of the flock under the shepherd's care, which closes the psalm that opened with beasts of the field eating the dead. The same pair appears in Ps 95:7 and 100:3.
